correctness.rationale: Verified the vertex-level quotient, the zero/one/two/three equality case partition, time-two eventual periodicity, exact disjointness and binomial weights of the three frozen-part choices. The fixed and already-periodic populations and complementary consensus basin identities were derived. The hypergeometric conditional law yields the ratio 1/sqrt(2) of Gaussian standard deviations and the stated angular constant. Two distinct standalone scripts, one over labelled bit configurations for n≤5, one over all count triples for n≤30, were replayed with recorded outputs reproduced; these support but do not replace the universal proof.

originality.rationale: The closest primary full text proves general finite eventual period at most two and studies infinite unimodular/random graphs; it does not imply a graph-specific two-step bound, strict-middle basin criterion, exact labelled basin sum, or square-root probability constant. The 1980 generalized threshold paper is historically prior for period bounds, not claimed as new. The new statements count eventual basin sizes rather than only initially periodic states; a targeted mathematical record search returned no stronger matching statement, without treating non-retrieval as proof of novelty. The 1980 full text was unavailable and its abstract was inspected, so historical priority remains qualified.
residual_risks: The entire 1980 generalized-threshold article was not inspected, so an example or special-case table in its body cannot be excluded.

value.rationale: The natural dynamical question is the probability that a random initial state is attracted to a genuine oscillation instead of consensus, not merely the count of states already periodic. The exact basin classification is uniform in n and exhibits a sharp square-root oscillation probability despite an exponentially small initially-periodic fraction. Both the count and constant are motivated natural invariants of a canonical dense modular graph, and require structural argument and a conditional central limit theorem, rather than merely changing a numerical parameter.
